svg.title: P021 · Top five customers by number of orders
svg.desc: One row per ranked buyer, including fifth-place ties. Nine order rows survive. Orders 17–19 retain ID 99 with NULL customer details. ID 7 has no orders and never enters the ranking. Nine orders form seven buyers. ID 99 contributes 3. IDs 1–6 contribute 1 each. The missing name becomes Unknown customer. Read the grouped buyers. Their counts are 3, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1. The fifth value sets the cutoff at 1. Every buyer reaches 1. All seven appear, including everyone tied for fifth. Sort tied buyers by customer ID. First inside customer_counts · FROM Orders. Only people who placed orders enter this ranking. The buyer ID written on each order is the value to count, even when its customer record is missing. Second · LEFT JOIN Customers. Match the order’s CustomerID to Customers for the name. The left join keeps all three orders for ID 99. A customer with zero orders, such as ID 7, supplies no ranking row. Outer query · FROM customer_counts. The CTE has one row per buyer ID. Reading it for the fifth-place cutoff compares buyers with buyers after all their orders have been counted.
svg.text: Top five customers by number of orders
One row per ranked buyer, including fifth-place ties.
Customer 99 has three orders and no customer record. Can that ID come first?
A triangle marks an example to follow. A dark source band spans its columns. ƒ marks a calculated value. Deeper cell colors mark the values to
follow. Double underlines mark the matching keys. SQL excerpts use … for omitted clauses.

Which count is in fifth place?

ORDER BY orders_placed DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 4
How many buyers meet that cutoff?
